A thorough understanding of pelvic anatomy and fracture patterns is critical for successful
management of acetabular injuries.
Defining acetabular injury via appropriate radiographs and CT scans is the foundation of an
effective treatment plan.
Restoration of a congruent and stable hip joint with an anatomically reduced articular surface
is associated with excellent long-term outcomes.
Epidemiology and Etiology
Acetabular fractures are associated with a bimodal age distribution.
Posterior wall fractures and associated both-column fractures are the most common injury
patterns.

Epidemiology and Etiology
The overall incidence of acetabular fractures is approximately 3 per 100,000 individuals
annually in the United States.1 Fractures of the acetabulum are associated with a
bimodal age distribution,1 with peaks in individuals in their twenties and fifties. In
younger patients, acetabular fractures result from high-energy trauma (most commonly
a motor vehicle collision) and are more likely to involve multisystem injuries.2 In elderly
patients, acetabular fractures usually are isolated injuries from low-energy mechanisms
(most commonly a ground-level fall).2 Overall, the most common fracture patterns are
isolated posterior wall fractures and associated both-column fractures.3
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The innominate bone is a condensation of the embryologic anlages of the pubis, ischium, and
ilium.
Acetabular fractures are classified and managed according to the two-column and inverted-Y
concept.
Major neurovascular structures surround the acetabulum.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The innominate bone is a condensation of the pubis, ischium, and ilium at the triradiate
cartilage, which fuse at the time of skeletal maturity.4 The plane of the ilium is
approximately 90° to the plane of the obturator foramen, and the articular surface of the
acetabulum is supported between the two limbs of an inverted Y of bone, as first
described by Letournel and Judet3 in their seminal work (Figure 1).
Figure 1 Schematic drawings show the anatomy of the innominate bone. A, At skeletal
maturity, the innominate bone is made up of the fused ischium, ilium, and pubis. Left,
Anterior articular view of the acetabulum (outside view). Right, View of the quadrilateral
surface of the acetabulum (inside view). The dashed lines demarcate the border of the
ilioischial column from the iliopectineal column. B, The two-column structural model of
the acetabulum, as described by Letournel, includes an anterior column and a posterior
column joined at the sciatic buttress in an inverted-Y shape. Left, outside view of the
anterior column (yellow) and the posterior column (orange). Right, inside view of the
posterior column (orange) and the anterior column (blue); the acetabulum is
represented by dashed lines. The sciatic buttress (black shading) connects both columns

to the axial skeleton through the sacroiliac joint. Illustrations show the vessels running
along the inner (C) and outer (D) table of the pelvis. (Reproduced with permission from
Letournel E, Judet R: Fractures of the Acetabulum, ed 2. New York, NY, Springer-Verlag,
1993, pp 4-21.)
The anterior column, or anterior limb of the inverted Y, consists of the anterior half of
the iliac wing, which is contiguous with the pelvic brim to the superior pubic ramus and
the anterior half of the acetabular articular surface.3 The posterior column, or posterior
limb of the inverted Y, begins at the superior aspect of the greater sciatic notch and is
contiguous with the greater and lesser sciatic notches inferiorly; it also includes the
ischial tuberosity.3 The two columns of bone are connected to the sacroiliac joint by a
thick strut of bone lying above the greater sciatic notch, known as the sciatic buttress.
The two columns meet medially to form the quadrilateral plate, which is the internal
cortical surface of the acetabulum. The superior portion of the acetabular articular
surface is referred to as the weight-bearing dome, or roof.5 This region extends from just
posterior to the anterior inferior iliac spine to the superior aspect of the posterior
column. The anterior and posterior walls of the acetabulum are components of the
respective columns. The cotyloid fossa is the central aspect of the medial wall of the
acetabulum that hosts the ligamentum teres and the fibrofatty pulvinar. The
nonarticular portion inside the U-shaped labrum extends to the acetabular notch, the
anteroinferior depression in the margin of the acetabulum bridged by the transverse
acetabular ligament.
Several major neurovascular structures pass through or adjacent to the pelvis near the
acetabulum, and the blood supply to the innominate bone is extensive. The external
surface receives its blood supply primarily from the superior gluteal artery (SGA), with
contributions from the inferior gluteal artery, the obturator artery, and the medial
femoral circumflex artery.5 Blood supply to the internal surface is derived from the
fourth lumbar, iliolumbar, and obturator arteries.5 The main nutrient artery to the ilium,
which originates from the iliolumbar artery, supplies the supra-acetabular region along
with branches of the SGA,6 whereas the posterior wall blood supply comes from
branches of the SGA and the inferior gluteal artery.5 The main blood supply to the
femoral head is the deep branch of the medial femoral circumflex artery,7 which is

Knowledge of the intrapelvic relationships of the nervous lumbosacral trunk, common
and external iliac vessels, inferior epigastric vessels, and obturator artery and nerve is
critical for safe surgical management. These neurovascular structures may be injured
during trauma or intraoperatively. The sciatic nerve also is vulnerable to injury as it
passes through and exits the greater sciatic notch, especially in patients with posterior

fracture-dislocations of the hip and acetabular fractures with posterior column or wall
displacement.9 At this level, the nerve typically separates into tibial and peroneal
components, with the peroneal division being more susceptible to injury. The superior
gluteal neurovascular bundle is found at the superior aspect of the greater sciatic notch.
This bundle courses between the gluteus minimus and medius and may adhere to bone
at different levels. Finally, fractures involving the sciatic buttress and/or greater notch
may injure the superior gluteal vessels, producing substantial hemorrhage that may
require embolization.
In the lateral portion of the superior pubic ramus, a retropubic vascular anastomosis
frequently traverses between the obturator, external iliac, and/or inferior epigastric
vasculature.10 A variation of this anastomosis, in which the origin of the inferior
epigastric artery comes from the obturator artery, is referred to as the corona mortis.11
These retropubic vascular anastamoses restrict mobilization of the external iliac vessel
during exposure. Damage to the vessels from an injury or during surgical approach may
cause hemorrhage that is challenging to control because of vessel retraction into the
obturator foramen.
Mechanism of Injury
The acetabulum is subjected to different forces with various modes of failure.
Acetabular fracture patterns depend on the position of the hip at the time of impact.

Mechanism of Injury
Fractures of the acetabulum are caused by impact of the femoral head with the
acetabular articular surface.12 This force to the femoral head may be applied via the
greater trochanter along the axis of the femoral neck or from anywhere along the axis of
the femoral shaft. Subsequently, the resulting acetabular fracture pattern depends on
the position of the hip at the time of impact and the location and direction of the
originally applied force3 (Figure 3). If the force is applied along the axis of the femoral
neck, external hip rotation produces an anterior fracture, whereas internal rotation

axis of the femur drives the femoral head against the posterior articular surface of the
acetabulum.4 With the addition of adduction, the femoral head may dislocate without
causing fracture. Regardless of hip position, the degree of fracture displacement,
fracture comminution, and articular impaction also depend on the magnitude of the
applied force and the quality of the underlying bone.
Patients with osteopenic or osteoporotic bone often sustain severely comminuted
fractures with articular impaction from low-energy injuries, such as falls. Typically,
geriatric acetabulum fractures involve the anterior column and/or wall because of a fall
onto the greater trochanter.2

Associated Injuries
Fractures of the acetabulum frequently are associated with other musculoskeletal, neurologic,
and visceral injuries.
Pelvic ring injuries associated with acetabular fractures present unique challenges.
If acetabular and femoral fractures occur in combination, surgical stages may be affected.
Neurologic injury of the ipsilateral extremity is common.

Associated Injuries
More than 50% of patients with acetabular fractures sustain other musculoskeletal,
neurologic, and/or visceral injuries.13 Lower extremity fractures are most common
(36%), followed by injuries to the lungs, retroperitoneum, and upper extremities.14 Other
concurrent injuries frequently involve the bowel, kidney, vascular system, bladder,
spleen, liver, brain, and spine.14 The incidence of associated injury tends to be lower in
geriatric patients than in younger patients because of the lower-energy mechanisms of
these fractures.2 However, 35% of elderly patients with an acetabular fracture require
transfusions, largely because of their increased risk for arterial injury.15
Concomitant disruption of the pelvic ring is estimated to occur in 9% of all patients with
an acetabular fracture.16 If combined, pelvic and acetabular injuries commonly are
associated with multiple system injuries, higher injury severity scores, and hypotension
on presentation,16,17 as well as higher rates of malreduction, failed fixation, and
malunion.18
Although the acetabulum has a vast and complex blood supply that is susceptible to
injury, clinicians should not presume that an isolated acetabulum fracture is the primary
cause of hypotensive shock;4 an alternative source of hemorrhage should be sought. If
the SGA or obturator artery is injured, therapeutic embolization via interventional
radiology is usually performed to control hemorrhage. Regardless, interventional
radiology procedures are controversial because they are associated with subsequent
wound breakdown and deep tissue infection after reconstructive surgery. Factors
contributing to increased wound complication rates after interventional radiology are

internal degloving or soft-tissue injury, bilateral versus unilateral procedures, selective
versus nonselective procedures, and permanent coiling versus embolization.19-21
In patients with acetabular fractures and associated ipsilateral fractures of the femur,
sequence and management strategies vary depending on the physiological condition of
the patient, soft-tissue injuries, and the location of the femoral fracture.22 Ipsilateral
femoral neck fractures should be managed promptly in young patients,23 and femoral
shaft fractures frequently are stabilized first to allow for manipulation and
reconstruction of the acetabulum.22 Finally, 15% to 30% of patients with an acetabular
fracture (most frequently, posterior wall fracture-dislocations) also sustain ligamentous
knee injuries; if a knee injury is suspected, MRI may be required for diagnosis and
further delineation.24
Neurologic injury to the ipsilateral lower extremity occurs in as many as 30% of patients
with an acetabular fracture.25 Injury to the sciatic nerve is most common and usually is
partial in nature, with the peroneal division most often affected. Prognosis for functional
recovery of the sciatic nerve is variable, with the tibial division more likely to achieve full
recovery, whereas the peroneal division tends to have a poor recovery.26 Other
peripheral nerves, such as the femoral, obturator, and gluteal nerves, may be injured
during acetabular fracture but typically have better prognosis for recovery.27 A recent
study on nerve root injuries associated with acetabular fractures managed surgically
found that L5 deficits recovered more predictably than S1 deficits.28
Fracture Classification
The most widely used classification system for acetabular fractures is the Letournel
classification.
Five elementary patterns of acetabular fractures exist: anterior column, posterior column,
anterior wall, posterior wall, and transverse patterns.
Five associated patterns exist: both columns, posterior column plus posterior wall, transverse
plus posterior wall, T-type, and anterior plus posterior hemitransverse patterns.

Fracture Classification
Anatomic classification systems help the surgeon gain a thorough understanding of
fracture patterns. This knowledge is important in determining whether surgical
management is required, and if so, the optimal surgical approach.3,29 The classification
of acetabulum fractures described by Letournel is the most widely used system.2,12 It
comprises five elementary patterns and five associated patterns (Figure 4).
Figure 4 Illustrations show the Judet and Letournel classification of acetabular fractures.
(Reproduced from Webb LX: Open reduction and internal fixation of posterior wall
acetabular fractures, in Colvin, AC, Flatow E, eds: Atlas of Essential Orthopaedic
Procedures, ed 2. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp
571-578.)
Elementary Patterns

Posterior wall (Figure 5)—This pattern disrupts the posterior rim of the acetabulum, a portion
of the retro-acetabular surface, and a segment of the articular cartilage.3,12 Posterior wall
fractures often are associated with instability of the femoral head (ie, dislocation or
subluxation) and marginal impaction of the articular cartilage and subchondral bone
(diagnosed via CT).30 Complex posterior wall fractures may involve the entire retro-acetabular
surface and a portion of the greater or lesser sciatic notch and the ischial tuberosity. The
ilioischial line remains intact on an AP view.
Figure 5 Pelvis radiographs demonstrate a posterior wall acetabular fracture. A, AP view
demonstrates that all radiographic landmarks are intact except the posterior rim (arrow). B,
Obturator oblique view demonstrates the displaced posterior wall fracture (arrow). C, Iliac
oblique view shows an intact posterior border. (Courtesy of Augustine M. Saiz, Jr, MD,
Sacramento, CA, and Jonathan G. Eastman, MD, Sacramento, CA.)
Posterior column (Figure 6)—This pattern disrupts the retro-acetabular surface and ischial
segments of the innominate bone, with a fracture of the ischiopubic ramus (inferior ramus)
that separates the posterior column from the anterior column.3,12 The retro-acetabular
surface frequently is displaced with the posterior column. Recall that the cranial extent of the
posterior column is the greater sciatic notch.

Anterior column (Figure 8)—The anterior column extends from the iliac crest to the anterior
half of the ischiopubic ramus; therefore, the cranial extent of an anterior column fracture can
be located from the dome of the acetabulum to the iliac crest. Four levels of fracture have
been described3,12: High fractures exit the iliac crest, intermediate fractures exit between the
anterior superior iliac spine and the anterior inferior iliac spine, low fractures exit below the
anterior inferior iliac spine, and very low fractures involve only the pubic portion of the
acetabulum. In all anterior column patterns, the fracture line must cross the pelvic brim
medially with disruption of the iliopectineal line and the ischiopubic ramus. Typically, medial
translation of the anterior column fragment occurs.
Figure 8 Pelvis radiographs demonstrate an anterior column acetabular fracture. A, AP view

ramus, thus separating the anterior column from the posterior column.3,12

Anterior plus posterior hemitransverse (Figure 14)—This pattern combines an anterior wall or

patterns is subtle. In the anterior plus posterior hemitransverse fracture pattern, the femoral
head typically follows the displacement of the anterior column, whereas in a T-shaped fracture
pattern, the femoral head typically follows the posterior column. The distinction between an
anterior plus posterior hemitransverse fracture and an associated both-column fracture also
may be difficult to discern; often, the fracture lines are nearly identical in orientation, with the
one key distinction being that an anterior plus posterior hemitransverse fracture pattern will
have some cartilage remaining attached to the intact ilium, whereas no cartilage remains
attached in the associated both-column fracture (Figure 15).

Associated both-column (Figure 16)—This fracture pattern represents a distinct category
defined by two necessary criteria: the primary fracture line separates the anterior and
posterior columns from each other and all articular segments are detached from the intact
portion of the posterior ilium.3,12 On radiographs, this fracture pattern has a pathognomonic
finding known as the spur sign. Best observed on an obturator oblique radiograph, the spur
represents the caudal edge of the intact posterior iliac wing separated from the medially
displaced articular segments.3,12

view demonstrates that, despite disruption of all six of the radiographic landmarks, the femoral
head remains congruent to the roof and the anterior column fragment. The position of the head

Patient History and Physical Examination
A patient history of the mechanism of injury obtained from the patient or first
responders may help predict a fracture pattern and associated injuries. Conscious
patients with an acetabular fracture typically report hip, knee, or leg pain. Often, these
patients have sustained high-energy trauma with associated injuries that must be
identified. In patients who were injured via a low-energy mechanism (eg, a ground-level
fall), an acetabular fracture usually is an isolated musculoskeletal injury in underlying
pathologic or osteoporotic bone. However, the reason for the fall must be determined
because a critical underlying cardiac or neurologic condition may be the cause,
particularly in elderly patients.
In any patient who sustains high-energy trauma, the physical examination should involve
standard Advanced Trauma Life Support protocol followed by a detailed tertiary survey
of the integument and soft tissues, musculoskeletal system, and neurovascular
system.31 The lower extremity, hip, and flank should be evaluated for open wounds or
closed, internal-degloving soft-tissue injuries (eg, Morel-Lavallee lesion). Open wounds
may communicate with the acetabular fracture, and extensive internal degloving lesions
may be secondarily colonized with pathogenic bacteria, leading to wound breakdown
and deep infection.32 Early diagnosis and management are important because these
wounds may require formal débridement followed by delayed closure and,
subsequently, delayed fracture fixation with alternative reduction/fixation strategies.32
A complete and documented neurologic examination of the lower extremity also is
critical in patients with an acetabular fracture because isolated sensory deficits and
weakness or total loss of movement of individual muscles may occur. Ideally, a
peripheral nerve examination is performed immediately on presentation, if possible, to
differentiate traumatic neurologic deficits from iatrogenic neurologic deficits. Peripheral
pulses with perfusion to the foot also should be verified via direct palpation or Doppler.

Overview
The classification and subsequent management of acetabular fractures are based on
imaging studies that provide a thorough understanding of innominate bone anatomy.
Judet and Letournel determined that the plane of the ilium is approximately 90° to the
plane of the obturator foramen and that both structures are oriented roughly 45° to the
frontal plane. They then demonstrated that an AP pelvis view and two 45°oblique views
(ie, Judet views) are sufficient for determining the radiographic anatomy of the
acetabulum.3,12
With improvements in imaging modalities and the introduction of CT, the evaluation of
acetabular fractures has advanced even more. Currently, more nuanced details and
improved understanding of anatomy, in part because of 3D reconstruction images,
facilitate surgeon assessment of acetabular injuries. Regardless, radiographic techniques
should continue to be taught because radiography is the preferred imaging modality for
verifying fracture reduction and joint congruency, especially intraoperatively.35

Plain radiography is essential for the diagnosis and assessment of acetabular fractures.
Accurate acetabular fracture classification also is possible via plain radiographs alone fractures

Intraoperative Dynamic Stress Views
In patients who have a small posterior wall fracture with or without a history of fracture-
dislocation and no free intra-articular fragments or areas of marginal impaction,
dynamic stress views are indicated to determine the stability of the hip joint.33,40 To
obtain such images, the patient is placed in the supine position with the hip in neutral
rotation and full extension. Intraoperatively, the fluoroscopic machine is positioned to
obtain an obturator oblique view. The hip is gradually flexed from 0° to 90° with
adduction and internal rotation, while a posteriorly directed manual force is applied
through the longitudinal axis of the femur. Sequentially, fluoroscopic images are
obtained at 0°, 30°, 60°, and 90° of flexion. If the hip remains congruent, imaging is
repeated with the addition of slight adduction and internal rotation (approximately
20°).39 Posterior subluxation is indicative of instability. After a posterior wall fracture, a
dynamic stress test under general anesthesia is the only method to reliably evaluate hip
stability.41

Management
Management of acetabular fractures is determined by patient- and fracture-related factors.
Similar to all articular injuries, a patient’s associated comorbidities and preinjury function are
important considerations.
The goal of management is optimal return of function via surgical or nonsurgical treatment.
In general, most acetabular fractures are managed surgically.
The goal of surgical management is to restore stability to a congruent hip while avoiding
complications.
After an acetabular fracture, the most important predictor of long-term outcomes is the
quality of reduction of the articular surface (<2 mm).

Patients with an acetabular fracture who meet certain conditions may have good outcomes
with nonsurgical treatment.
Occasionally, nonsurgical treatment is selected because of a patient’s condition.

Techniques/Procedures
Nonsurgical management of acetabular fractures typically involves weight-of-leg– and foot-
flat–weight bearing with the use of assistive devices, with serial radiographs obtained over the
first 8 weeks and weight bearing gradually advanced to full–weight bearing at 12 weeks.
Prolonged traction should be considered only in patients with surgical indications related to
fracture displacement but with contraindications to surgical treatment. In these patients,
traction should be maintained until the fracture has healed enough to allow for progressive
weight-bearing ambulation, typically 4 to 12 weeks.47

In a study of 49 patients with a nondisplaced linear or medial wall fracture not involving

Surgical Timing
Acetabular fractures may be managed promptly (ie, within 48 hours postinjury) without
an increased risk of blood loss or complications.52 In general, the surgical management
of acetabular fractures is not an emergency. A delay of 3 to 5 days is common to allow
for evaluation of any underlying medical problems or associated injuries and for
preoperative planning. However, a delay of more than 10 days from injury to surgical
reduction or reconstruction of acetabulum fractures is a considerable predictor of
negative radiologic and clinical outcomes.53,54 Reduction techniques rely on
manipulation of relatively mobile fracture fragments; by 10 days postinjury, organization
of the hematoma and early fracture healing begins to limit this mobility. By 2 weeks
postinjury, healing often has progressed to the point that fracture mobility is lost, and a
more extensive surgical approach is required. After 3 weeks postinjury, callus formation
is extensive, and the fracture is no longer considered acute.3
In a study by Dailey et al,53 patients with an acetabular fracture in whom anatomic
reduction was achieved after ORIF had shorter delays from injury to surgical
management (median delay, 3 days) than patients in whom imperfect reduction was
achieved (median delay, 4.5 days) or patients in whom poor reduction was achieved
(median delay, 7 days). The odds of anatomic reduction decreased by 12% each day that
surgical intervention was delayed after injury.53 Therefore, surgical management should
be performed as soon as safely possible and should not be delayed more 15 days
postinjury for fractures with elementary patterns or more than 10 days postinjury for
fractures with associated patterns.53

Patient Positioning
During acetabular fracture repair, patient positioning depends on the surgical approach
selected. For most anterior approaches, such as the ilioinguinal, AIP, iliofemoral, and
Heuter approaches, the patient is positioned flat and supine with the ipsilateral hip
flexed to approximately 30° or more. A midline sacral bump may be used if
percutaneous fixation of associated posterior pelvic ring injuries is required.
For posterior approaches, such as the Kocher-Langenbeck or Gibson approaches, lateral
or prone patient positioning may be used, depending on the fracture pattern and patient
characteristics. Isolated posterior wall fractures are easily managed via lateral patient
positioning, which facilitates soft-tissue retraction; however, with transverse fractures,
lateral patient positioning tends to displace the fracture; therefore, prone patient
positioning often is preferred. Theoretically, prone patient positioning helps protect the
sciatic nerve because the hip stays extended and the knee remains flexed.
For the extended iliofemoral approach, the lateral position affords simultaneous access
to the anterior and posterior columns.

Open Reduction and Internal Fixation
Achieving anatomic reduction of acetabular fractures is beneficial for outcome and
stable fixation. Multiple dedicated forceps are available to facilitate reduction, with the
two main styles involving tines (ie, Weber, angled jaw clamps) or screw assistance (ie,
Jungbluth or Farabeuf clamps). Spiked-ball pushers, with and without disks to increase
surface area contact, are particularly useful for manipulating fracture fragments.
Alternatively, Schanz pins inserted into major fracture fragments may help control
rotational displacements, similar to a joystick. Reduction is then assessed via direct
visualization, palpation of fracture lines, and fluoroscopic imaging.
The design of a fixation construct using different combinations of 3.5-mm cortical screws
and pelvic reconstruction plates is based on the individual fracture; however, the design
may be generalized. Lag or positional screws are used to replace reduction clamps and
maintain reduction of columns and major fracture fragments. Neutralization plates
stabilize columns, and buttress plates stabilize wall fragments. Reconstruction plates are
more malleable than standard small-fragment compression plates, allowing for over- or
under-contouring, which may be helpful for indirect reduction techniques and
compression. Locking plates may limit the screw placement trajectory and have not been
shown to improve stability, even in osteoporotic bone; therefore, their use is limited in
this setting. Some studies have suggested that quadrilateral surface implants spanning
the anterior and posterior columns are biomechanically superior; however, their use in
vivo has not been studied66 (Figure 27).

Percutaneous Techniques
Percutaneous fixation techniques have many indications in acetabular fracture
management. Elderly or very sick patients with multiple comorbidities that preclude
prolonged surgical reduction and fixation may notably benefit from percutaneous
stabilization of the columns, which stabilizes the femoral head, allowing for immediate
mobilization and preventing complications from bed immobilization. This procedure is
particularly appropriate if irreparable articular damage will require future arthroplasty.
In young patients with good bone quality, percutaneous fixation techniques prevent
displacement of nondisplaced fractures. Transtectal fracture lines are particularly prone
to displacement with nonsurgical management, considered the worst possible outcome.
Percutaneous fixation is particularly useful if a patient cannot be followed up on a
routine basis or is unlikely to adhere to treatment. Percutaneous techniques also may
provide anterior and posterior column fixation; however, they are not useful for wall
fixation (Figure 28).

Urgent THA
In the past decade, the incidence of acetabular fractures in patients older than 65 years
has increased substantially.2 In this patient population, fractures often result from a low-
energy fall onto the patient’s side and typically are variants of the anterior plus posterior
hemitransverse or associated both-column pattern.69 These variants are predominantly
characterized by anterior column displacement (with a low exit caudal to the anterior
superior iliac spine), involvement of the quadrilateral surface, and intrapelvic
medialization of the femoral head. Superior-medial dome impaction (the gull sign) and
superior-lateral femoral head impaction frequently accompany these injuries because of
poor bone quality.70 In medically compromised and elderly patients with poor bone
quality, a fall onto the knee may also cause an isolated posterior wall fracture; however,

In patients with acetabular fractures, the goal of postoperative management is early
mobilization.
Mechanical and chemical prophylaxis for venous thromboembolism (VTE) is recommended in
patients without contraindications.

Postoperative Management
After reduction and fixation of acetabular fractures, reduction quality and safe
placement (extra-articular) of fixation should be evaluated fluoroscopically.
Intraoperative or postoperative CT may be used to assess reduction of the articular
surface and asses for missed intra-articular fragments or fixation; however, this practice
is controversial because of concerns for post-radiation sarcoma, and the low rate of
revision after postoperative CT makes such imaging hard to justify unless postoperative
plain radiographs are concerning.
The patient should remain weight-of-leg– and foot-flat–weight bearing for at least 6 to 12
weeks postoperatively, depending on bone quality, stability of fixation, and degree of
articular involvement. Early hip range of motion with physical therapy and/or a
continuous passive motion machine is encouraged, and abductor strengthening
exercises can begin at 3 to 4 weeks postoperatively. Given that no contraindications
exist, VTE prophylaxis should be initiated after admission and continued for at least 4
weeks postoperatively.
Prophylaxis against heterotopic ossification is not routine but should be considered in
patients at high risk for heterotopic ossification (ie, patients with electrocution, burn, or
head injuries; prolonged ventilation use; and extensive abductor muscle devitalization).
Radiation therapy (one dose of 650 to 750 cGy within 48 hours) is considered the most
reliable form of heterotopic ossification prophylaxis. Indomethacin has not been shown
to decrease the incidence of clinically important heterotopic ossification (Brooker class III

Outcomes of ORIF
In patients with acetabular fractures, excellent outcomes are expected with quality reduction.

Outcomes of ORIF
Results after ORIF of acetabular fractures vary in the literature and often are difficult to
interpret; however, three of the largest series investigating outcomes of acetabular
fractures managed via ORIF within 3 weeks postinjury reported good or excellent results
in 75% to 81% of the fractures at long-term follow-up.3,29,81,82 All the studies agreed that
the quality of reduction directly correlated with the final clinical result. Posttraumatic
arthritis occurred after 10 to 25 years in only 10% of the patients in whom reduction was
graded as perfect, whereas posttraumatic arthritis occurred within the first 10 years in
36% of the patients with imperfect reduction.3

improvement in outcomes with early THA in patients in whom posttraumatic arthritis
develops; however, one study reported that patients who underwent THA had lower
functional scores than those who did not undergo conversion to THA after successful

Complications
Acetabular fractures are associated with medical and surgical complications.
After acetabular fracture repair, early mobilization is encouraged to prevent complications
from prolonged recumbency (ie, pulmonary and urinary tract infections, gastrointestinal
complications, and VTE).
Complications associated with acetabular fractures have been the focus of recent research.
Post-traumatic arthritis is the most important complication. A comprehensive long-term
follow-up study on hip survivorship in patients with surgically managed fractures reported a
20-year hip survivorship rate of 79% after ORIF.73
In a retrospective review of 12 patients who underwent angiographic embolization of pelvic
arterial hemorrhage before ORIF, postoperative deep infections occurred in 58% of
patients.19 Those most at risk had nonselective coiling of the bilateral internal iliac system.
Although the efficacy of intraoperative red blood cell salvage is cost effective in acetabular
surgery, the amount of blood returned to the patient is relatively low and its effect on
decreasing allogeneic transfusion has not been proven.85-87
Patients with an acetabular fracture have a high risk for deep vein thrombosis; however, the
use of prophylactic anticoagulation and mechanical prophylaxis decreases this risk. In
patients with a contraindication to systemic chemoprophylaxis, the risk for pulmonary
embolism may be decreased with use of inferior vena cava filters.88,89 Retrievable inferior
vena cava filters provide temporary protection from pulmonary embolism and prevent the
long-term complications associated with the use of permanent filters (ie, recurrent deep vein
thrombosis, chronic venous stasis disease, organ penetration, vena cava thrombosis, and
filter migration).90,91 The historical reported retrieval rate for these filters was 34%; however,
dedicated protocols and clinics have increased the retrieval rate to 60%.92
Heterotopic ossification may greatly affect outcomes. Historically, risk factors for heterotopic
ossification included traumatic brain injury, the use of an extensile surgical approach, and a
fracture requiring dual approaches, with additional risk factors continuing to be identified. In
addition, mechanical ventilation for 72 hours or more has been identified as a risk factor for
severe heterotopic ossification.93

Pearls and Pitfalls
Acetabular fractures have a bimodal age distribution, with younger patients more likely to
experience high-energy trauma and older patients more likely to experience low-energy
trauma.
Acetabular osteology is unique, with the innominate bone surrounded by major neurovascular
structures.
The physical examination for acetabular fractures should include standard Advanced Trauma
Life Support protocol and evaluation for frequently associated injuries.
Vigilance for hip dislocations also is required.
AP and Judet oblique radiographs are used in the diagnosis of acetabular fractures. The six key
radiographic landmarks should be identified and assessed.
Axial and reformatted CT scans further aid in classifying fracture pattern and fragment
morphology.
Optimal management of acetabular fractures requires an appropriate preoperative plan based
on a thorough understanding of all fracture lines and fragments and individual patient
variables.

Posterior wall fractures in patients with a history of dislocation are assumed to be unstable
until proven otherwise via dynamic stress testing under general anesthesia.
The goals of acetabular fracture management are to attain and maintain a stable, congruent,
and anatomic hip socket and to avoid complications.
In limited circumstances, nonsurgical management of acetabular fractures may be
appropriate.
Most displaced acetabular fractures should be managed surgically, with the goals of anatomic
reduction, tissue-sparing dissection, and stable fixation that allows for early motion.
The role of percutaneous-only fixation and combined emergent ORIF/THA has not been fully
determined.
Complications are not uncommon in patients with an acetabular fracture and include wound
disorders, VTE, heterotopic ossification, iatrogenic nerve injury, and post-traumatic arthritis.
The quality of reduction is the most important predictor of hip survivorship.
